title: Psalm 75: God Brings One Down and Exalts Another
summary: The congregation gives thanks because God's Name is near, and God himself answers: at the time he chooses he will judge fairly, holding the trembling earth steady and warning the arrogant not to raise their horns. The psalmist declares that exaltation comes from God alone, who holds a cup of foaming wine that the wicked must drain. The psalm ends with a vow of praise and God's promise to cut off the horns of the wicked and lift up the righteous.
story: Psalm 75 follows the anguished laments of Psalms 73 and 74. Psalm 74 asked how long God would allow the enemy to mock him and pleaded with him to rise up; Psalm 75 answers with God's own voice announcing that he will judge at the appointed time. The movement from lament to divine answer is part of how Book III is arranged, and it keeps the questions of Psalms 73 and 74 from having the last word. The psalm also picks up a theme that runs through the whole Bible, from Hannah's song to Mary's: God humbles the proud and lifts up the lowly.
historical: The heading reads “For the choirmaster: To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Psalm of Asaph. A song.” The tune name Do Not Destroy (Hebrew al tashcheth) also appears over Psalms 57, 58, and 59. It was probably the opening words of a known melody, though some connect it with Moses' prayer that God would not destroy his people (Deuteronomy 9:26). For Asaph and his guild of Levitical singers, see Psalm 73. The psalm names no historical event, and its date is unknown. Some scholars link it, along with Psalm 76, to a moment of deliverance for Jerusalem such as the Assyrian retreat in 701 BC, but others read it as a liturgical psalm used in temple worship without reference to any single event. Its placement right after Psalm 74 suggests that the editors of the Psalter heard it as God's answer to the lament over the ruined sanctuary.
cultural:
The horn was a common symbol of strength and dignity, drawn from the image of a wild ox or ram tossing its head. To lift up one's horn meant to act with pride or defiance, and to have one's horn exalted meant to be honored and made strong (1 Samuel 2:1, 10). An outstretched or stiff neck was an image of arrogance and stubbornness. The pillars of the earth (verse 3) reflect the ancient picture of the world as a structure resting on foundations, which God holds steady even when everything trembles.

The cup in verse 8 draws on the custom of a host passing a cup to guests. In the prophets the cup of God's wrath became a vivid image of judgment: nations are made to drink wine that makes them stagger and fall (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15-16). The wine here is foaming and mixed with spices, strong and intoxicating, and the wicked must drink it down to the dregs, the bitter sediment at the bottom of the cup.
literary: The psalm alternates voices. The congregation speaks in verse 1, God speaks in verses 2 to 5 (the BSB marks this with quotation marks), a single worshiper reflects in verses 6 to 9, and God's voice returns in verse 10. This mix of human and divine speech gives the psalm the feel of a liturgy in which a prophet or priest delivered God's answer in the temple. The theme is carried by the word exalt (rum), which appears in verses 4, 5, 6, 7, and 10, and by the horn, which is lifted in pride in verses 4 and 5 and exalted by God in verse 10. The psalm turns on verse 7: God judges, bringing one down and lifting up another.

outline.t: God speaks: I will judge fairly
Exaltation comes from God; the cup of judgment
A vow of praise and God's promise

doctrines.note: God judges at the time he chooses, not the time people demand. The psalm reassures those tempted by the delay (as in Psalm 73) that judgment will come and will be fair.
God holds up the pillars of the earth when it trembles, and he alone brings one down and lifts another up. Human power and status are given and taken by him.

words.note: Qeren, horn. A symbol of strength, honor, and defiant pride. The wicked lift up their horns against heaven, but God will cut them off and exalt the horns of the righteous. The image appears in Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:10) and later in Zechariah's praise of a horn of salvation (Luke 1:69).

Rum, to be high, to lift up, or to exalt. The key verb of the psalm, it is used both for the arrogant lifting themselves up and for God exalting the righteous. The difference lies in who does the lifting.
Kos, cup. In verse 8 it is the cup of God's wrath. The image recurs through the prophets and into the New Testament, where it becomes the cup Jesus prays might pass from him.
Moed, an appointed time or season. It is the word used for Israel's appointed feasts. In verse 2 God says he chooses the time of judgment, which answers the anxious How long of Psalm 74.

christ: The New Testament doesn't quote Psalm 75, but its imagery runs deep in the story of Jesus. Mary's song praises God who has brought down rulers from their thrones and lifted up the humble (Luke 1:52), and Zechariah blesses God for raising up a horn of salvation in the house of David (Luke 1:69). Most strikingly, the cup of God's wrath poured for the wicked becomes the cup Jesus prays about in Gethsemane: “Take this cup from Me” (Mark 14:36). Christians have long read that moment as Jesus drinking the cup of judgment in the place of sinners. Revelation takes up the same image of the wine of God's wrath poured full strength for those who worship the beast (Revelation 14:10). The psalm is not predicting these events, but it gives the New Testament a vocabulary for what Christ did.
questions: The psalm says exaltation comes from God, not from east or west. Where are you tempted to look for honor or status apart from God?
God says he will judge at the time he chooses. How does that shape your patience when evil seems to go unpunished?
Christians read the cup of wrath in light of Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane. What does it mean to you that Jesus drank a cup meant for others?
